t-coc.sum: A document in which the supplier signs to confirm that the ordered product conforms to the standard and order conditions. Because it is a declaration without test values, it cannot prove properties by itself and is supported by attached certificates and traceability information.
facts: ISO 16228 F2.1 (declaration of compliance for fasteners) is a document that declares compliance without test values, and is confirmed and signed by an authorized person of the manufacturer or distributor.
EN 10204 2.1 is also a declaration of compliance without test values, but the issuer is limited to the manufacturer.

What a CoC can state: the order standard, quantity, lot (heat) number, list of attached documents, and the scope the supplier confirmed. What it cannot state: values of tests it did not perform, and specific inspection results at the 3.1 level.
ISO 16228 documents are valid only for the condition at the time of delivery. If further processing such as coating is done after delivery, part or all of the content may become invalid.

Unless otherwise agreed, even if documents are received, the responsibility for incoming inspection lies with the buyer (ISO 3269), and the responsibility for traceability after the original packaging is opened is also borne by the buyer (ISO 16228).
watch: "CoC provided" means a document without test values. If tensile, hardness, or composition values are needed, specify 3.1 (or F3.1) or an accredited test certificate separately.
If a CoC says "manufacturer's 3.1 attached", check that the heat number of the attached 3.1 connects to the lot number and product marking on the CoC.
ISO 16228 requires the document type to be decided at the time of ordering. If requested after shipment, the necessary tests and traceability records may not exist.

t-heat-lot.sum: The heat number is the number of the unit of steel made in a single melt, and the lot is a product unit grouped by the same heat, the same diameter, and the same heat treatment. It is the key connecting certificates and products, so the numbers on markings, labels, and documents must be the same.
facts: Chemical composition is set per heat, and mechanical properties differ by heat treatment lot and diameter. So one certificate usually represents one "heat + diameter + heat treatment lot".

ISO 16228 requires that fasteners can be traced to the end by the manufacturing lot number (or traceability lot number) and that manufacturing lots are not mixed. The manufacturing lot number is always included in F3.1 and F3.2.
A supplier that has issued an ISO 16228 document keeps the process and final inspection records for at least 3 years.
In EN 10204, when a distributor passes on a certificate, it attaches a means of identifying the product so that traceability between product and documents is not broken.
Marking the heat number directly on the product is often not an obligation of the product standard, so if needed, write "heat number (or traceability code) marking" in the order specification.
watch: If multiple heats are mixed in one box, one certificate cannot describe the entire box. Request that packaging and labels be divided by heat.
If the product has no marking and the number is only on the label, traceability is broken the moment the packaging is opened. Store them separated by heat until installation.
Even with the same heat, mechanical values differ if the diameter or heat treatment lot differs. Check that the value for the delivered diameter is on the certificate.
Under ISO 16228, the responsibility for traceability after the original packaging is opened passes to the buyer.

t-marking.sum: The grade symbols and manufacturer identification symbols stamped on bolt heads, stud ends, and nut faces. High-strength products with a grade but no manufacturer's symbol cannot be traced to their source and are treated with suspicion.
facts: ISO 898-1, 898-2, and ISO 3506 require marking the property class (8.8, 10, A2-70, etc.) and the manufacturer identification symbol, and for small diameters it applies from the size set by the standard.
SAE J429 indicates the grade by the number of radial lines on the head. Grade 5 has 3 lines and Grade 8 has 6 lines.
In ISO 10684 hot-dip galvanizing, overtapped nuts are additionally marked with Z (6AZ) or X (6AX) after the strength marking, and undersized bolts with U.
watch: High-strength bolts with only a grade symbol and no manufacturer's symbol cannot be traced to their source. For plant bolting, keep photos of the markings and compare them with the manufacturer that issued the certificate.
Cutting the end of a stud to shorten the length may remove the marking. Before cutting, check that the remaining end has a marking.
To avoid mixing galvanized B7 with unplated B7, check the markings and labels together with the coating entry on the certificate.

head: Marking
Meaning
rows: ASTM F3125 structural bolts (Type 3 is underlined)
Z · X after strength / U on bolt
table.note: Actual markings also include the manufacturer identification symbol (RCSC 2025 figure: XYZ = manufacturer's symbol). The F3125 · A194 2H markings are based on the RCSC 2025 figure.

t-pmi.sum: A procedure that measures the alloy composition of a part with an on-site analyzer to confirm that the specified material is correct. It only distinguishes the material family by alloying elements and does not tell heat treatment, hardness, or strength.
facts: Handheld XRF quickly measures alloying elements such as Cr · Ni · Mo · V but cannot measure light elements such as carbon.
Spark OES can measure up to carbon but grinds the surface and leaves discharge marks, so choose a measurement position that is not the threaded portion or bearing face.

B7 and B7M are usually made of the same family of steel (4140, etc.) and are distinguished by heat treatment and hardness, so they are not distinguished even by an analysis that measures carbon. Confirm by hardness results and markings.
304 and 316 (A2 · A4 series) are distinguished by Mo. Materials that differ only in carbon content, such as 304 and 304L, and 316 and 316L, cannot be distinguished by XRF.
Material verification programs for refinery and petrochemical facilities often refer to API RP 578.
A PMI result is only a confirmation of the material family and does not replace an EN 10204 certificate.
watch: A "PMI done" mark is meaningful only if there is a record of who measured which part with what equipment. Require the equipment type, measured elements, and acceptance criteria on the result sheet.
The claim that B7M was confirmed by PMI does not hold. Confirm B7M by hardness test records and markings.
It is normal for an XRF result to have no carbon. If confirmation of L grades (low carbon) is needed, specify a method that can measure carbon.

t-kolas.sum: A certificate issued by a laboratory accredited under ISO/IEC 17025 by the Korea Laboratory Accreditation Scheme (KOLAS), operated by the Korean Agency for Technology and Standards, for tests within the accredited scope. The results apply only to the specimens tested.
facts: The issuer is not the manufacturer but the laboratory. It is a different type from EN 10204 3.1: a document of test results from an independent laboratory.
The results apply only to the specimens submitted by the requester. If the specimens must represent the lot, have the laboratory or inspection body take the samples itself.
Even within one certificate, items outside the accredited scope may be mixed in. Distinguish items bearing the accreditation mark from those that do not.

The accredited scope (test items and test standards) differs by body, so before requesting, check that the accreditation certificate lists the relevant standard (e.g., ISO 898-1, ASTM F606, ASTM A370).

KOLAS is an accreditation body that has signed the ILAC and APAC mutual recognition arrangements (MRA), so in principle a certificate within the accredited scope is accepted overseas as an accredited test result. The final acceptance is decided by the purchaser.
The accreditation mark concerns the test result and does not mean product certification or quality assurance.

Test items common on bolt certificates: product tensile, proof load, wedge tensile, hardness, chemical composition, Charpy impact, decarburization, plating thickness, salt spray. The accredited scope differs by laboratory.
watch: Check that the sample name, standard, and lot marking on the certificate connect to the delivered product. A certificate whose sample name is only "bolt" cannot describe the delivered lot.
Forgery or alteration of certificates is prohibited by the Act on Conformity Assessment Management, etc. (Korea). Attaching the same certificate to another lot cannot prove that lot.

Attaching a KOLAS test does not make it EN 10204 3.2. 3.2 is a manufacturer's document prepared and signed jointly by the manufacturer's authorized inspection representative and the buyer's (or statutory) inspector.
Test items not in the accredited scope come out as non-accredited results even from the same laboratory. For special tests, check whether they are accredited before requesting.

t-tensile.t: Tensile test (tensile strength · yield strength · elongation)
t-tensile.sum: A test that pulls a specimen or a whole bolt until it breaks to measure tensile strength, yield strength, elongation, and reduction of area. The TS · YS · EL · RA fields on a certificate are these results.
facts: Tensile strength is the maximum load divided by the cross-sectional area, and yield strength is usually set at the 0.2 % permanent deformation point (0.2 % offset, Rp0.2).

Bolts are measured in two ways: product tensile, which pulls the whole product (based on the stress area of the threaded portion), and tensile of a specimen machined from the bolt or bar. Yield strength, elongation, and reduction of area are mainly measured on specimens.
Test methods are in ASTM A370 · F606/F606M (fasteners), ISO 898-1 (metric property classes, including test methods), and ISO 6892-1 (metallic materials in general).

The overview of the current edition of ASTM A193 covers full-size wedge tensile testing of the product together with specimen tensile requirements. In the wedge test, it must not break at the head-shank junction.
watch: When comparing elongation with the standard minimum, check that the gauge length of the specimen is the same as that standard's basis.
The tensile values on a bar certificate are based on that bar's diameter. For products of a diameter different from the certificate, check again against the criteria by diameter range.
Some grades have only a minimum, but others have an upper limit (e.g., F3125 A490 has tensile 150–173 ksi). A value that is too high may also fail.
When converting ksi to MPa, 1 ksi = 6.895 MPa.

t-proof-test.sum: A product test that applies the specified proof load and releases it, then checks that the bolt has no permanent elongation and the nut threads are not stripped. It confirms the properties in the region just below yield on the actual product.
facts: Proof load = proof stress × stress area of the threaded portion. The proof stress is set slightly lower than the yield strength.
The ISO 898-1 bolt proof load test applies the proof load and releases it, then compares the bolt length with that before loading to check that there is no permanent elongation.
ASTM F606/F606M provides the length measurement method, yield strength method, and uniform hardness method for the bolt proof load test.
The nut is fitted on a test mandrel (or test bolt) and the proof load is applied; the threads must not be stripped or broken.
Overtapped hot-dip galvanized nuts have reduced thread engagement, so the proof load is lower. ISO 10684 separately specifies the reduced values for M8 · M10 overtapped nuts.
watch: If the certificate only says "proof load passed" with no load value or diameter, ask with what load it was tested.

Some standards confirm properties by specimen tensile and hardness instead of proof load. If the certificate has no proof load field, first check the standard requirements to see whether it is an omission.
If an overtapped nut is mated with a general bolt, the engagement is insufficient and it may not withstand the proof load.

Proof stress
Basis
table.note: Proof load = proof stress × stress area. Values are from ISO 898-1:2013 Table 3.

t-wedge.sum: A product tensile test that places an inclined wedge under the bolt head and pulls until it breaks, to check that the head-shank junction does not break first even under a load mixed with bending.
facts: The wedge tilts the head to one side and adds bending to the fillet under the head. If there is overhardening, poor heat treatment, or a defect in the fillet, it breaks at the head junction.
There are two acceptance criteria. The minimum tensile load of the grade must be reached, and the fracture must occur in the shank or threaded portion, not in the head or the head-shank junction.
The wedge angle is set by the standard table, and test methods are in ISO 898-1, ASTM F606/F606M, and ASTM A370.
The ISO 898-1 wedge tensile test is for bolts and screws with a head (studs excluded). Studs are usually confirmed by axial product tensile or specimen tensile.
For products too short to apply a wedge, confirm by other tests set by the standard (hardness, head soundness test, etc.).
watch: When replacing 10.9, 12.9, or SAE Grade 8 bolts with products from another supplier, if there are only product tensile results, the toughness of the head junction may not have been confirmed. Check whether wedge results exist.
A wedge test result that does not state the fracture location has only half of its basis for judgment. Require the fracture location to be stated.

t-hardness.t: Hardness (HRC · HRB · HBW · HV) and conversion
t-hardness.sum: The quickest test for confirming the heat treatment condition of a bolt. There are four scales with different indenters and loads, and conversion table values are approximations, so judge by the measured value on the scale set by the standard.
facts: HRC is Rockwell hardness measuring indentation depth with a diamond cone and 150 kgf, and HRB with a 1/16" ball and 100 kgf. HRC is used in the range of about 20 and above, and HRB in the range of about 100 and below.

HBW is Brinell hardness obtained from the diameter of the indentation of a tungsten carbide ball (test force up to 29.42 kN = 3000 kgf), and replaces the HB · HBS notation of old editions that used a steel ball.
HV is Vickers hardness obtained from the indentation of a diamond square pyramid, used for comparing surface and core and for small parts.
Conversion uses the tables of ASTM E140 · ISO 18265, but there is error depending on steel type and heat treatment, so do not decide acceptance by conversion for values near the upper limit.
If the surface is too hard compared with the core, suspect carburization; if soft, decarburization. ISO 898-1 tests the two separately.
watch: If a certificate for a soft grade has only an HRC value, below 20 HRC is outside the recommended range of the HRC scale, so request HB · HRB results separately.
The value differs by measurement position (on the head, at the thread end, at the section center). Check that it is the value at the position set by the standard.
Hardness measured on plating or coating comes out low. Measure at a place where the coating has been removed.
Values from on-site portable hardness testers have large conversion errors, so check them against a reference specimen before using them for judgment.

table.note: ISO values are from ISO 898-1:2013, the sour limit from the NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 interpretation (A.2.1.2), and ISO 4042 is based on the 2022 edition. The hardness range is judged by the measured value on the scale set by the standard.

t-charpy.sum: A test in which a V-notched specimen is cooled to a specified temperature and broken in a single blow by a pendulum, and the absorbed energy is measured. It is the evidence that bolts and nuts do not fracture in a brittle manner at low temperature.
facts: The standard specimen is 10 × 10 × 55 mm with a 2 mm deep V-notch. For thin material from which a standard specimen cannot be obtained, subsize specimens 7.5, 5 and 2.5 mm thick are used.
Current A320 states that when L43 is specified to meet the Table 2 impact absorbed energy at −101 °C (−150 °F), further composition limits, such as a lower P and S, may be needed.
A320 requires the nut material used with the bolting to be impact tested as well.
Some specifications also look at lateral expansion or the percentage of ductile fracture surface in addition to absorbed energy. The test methods are ASTM E23 and A370, and ISO 148-1.
watch: Compare the impact test temperature on the certificate with the minimum design metal temperature (MDMT). Whether it is acceptable is decided by the test temperature and exemption rules set by the applicable code or specification.
L7 is a low-temperature grade supplied with impact testing. Check that the L7 certificate has the impact values and the test temperature.
If a low-temperature bolt is paired with an ordinary 2H nut, the toughness of the nut side is not confirmed. Match it with a nut that is also impact tested.

t-mdmt.sum: The minimum design metal temperature shown together with the MAWP on the nameplate of an ASME VIII Div.1 pressure vessel. For the bolting as well, the impact test requirements are worked out from this temperature, and the A193 or A320 grade and the matching nut are selected accordingly.
facts: Conditions colder than the operating temperature often set the MDMT, such as auto-refrigeration when pressure is released, or winter ambient air.

The ASME VIII-1 interpretation (2002, 1991) answers that the MDMT is the value shown on the nameplate together with the MAWP, and that the nameplate may show an MDMT warmer than the value determined by the test and exemption rules.

ASME VIII-1 interpretation VIII-1-01-25 (2001): SA-320 L7, L7A and L43 impact tested at −150 °F, and SA-194 Grade 4 and 7 nuts with the supplementary low-temperature impact requirement, can be used at an MDMT of −150 °F (converted −101 °C) or above.
ASME VIII-1 interpretation VIII-81-68 (1981): SA-193 B7 under 2-1/2" must also be impact tested, or fall under a UCS-66 exemption provision, to be used down to −50 °F (converted −46 °C).

Marine low-temperature piping (46 CFR 56.50-105) requires Charpy testing at a temperature at least 10 °F below the minimum service temperature, and for bolting requires an average of 20 ft·lbf for L7 and L43 down to −150 °F.
watch: If the datasheet has only the design temperature and the MDMT is blank, it cannot be judged whether low-temperature bolting is needed. Get the MDMT before quoting.
A common mistake is to change only the bolt to L7 and leave the nut as 2H. Match it with a nut that is also impact tested (A320 1.4).

t-sour.sum: Conditions that limit material and hardness to prevent sulfide stress cracking (SSC), in which high-strength steel absorbs hydrogen in a wet H2S environment and suddenly fractures. For bolting, the grade differs depending on whether it is "exposed" to the sour environment.
facts: The reference is NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 (oil and gas production), and refineries often use NACE MR0103/ISO 17945. ISO 15156-2 covers carbon and low-alloy steels, and ISO 15156-3 covers corrosion-resistant alloys.
For carbon and low-alloy steels, ISO 15156-2 sets general conditions such as 22 HRC or less, nickel under 1 %, and not being a free-machining steel.

For exposed bolting (bolting that is cut off from the atmosphere by insulation, burial or a flange cover, or that contacts the fluid), reduced-hardness grades such as A193 B7M and A320 L7M + A194 2HM and 7M are commonly used.
For flange bolting fully exposed to the atmosphere, using B7/2H is common practice, but whether it applies is decided by the project specification.
Plating or PTFE coating cannot substitute for an unsuitable material.
watch: If the specification says only "NACE", first confirm whether it is MR0175 or MR0103, and whether the bolting is exposed or non-exposed.
Wrapping with insulation or covering the flange with a cover changes non-exposed bolting into exposed bolting.
For a B7M certificate, check the hardness results, and if a value below 20 HRC is given only in HRC, get it again in HB or HRB.

L43 is of the AISI 4340 family, so its nickel is usually 1.65–2.00 %, above 1 %, and it does not fall under the general conditions for carbon and low-alloy steels in ISO 15156-2; it is therefore not used as exposed sour bolting.
B7M cannot be distinguished from B7 by PMI. Confirm it by the markings and the hardness records.

Remarks

table.note: General combinations (grade names only; check hardness values in the current edition of each standard). The applicable standard (MR0175 or MR0103) and the project specification take precedence.

t-hydrogen.sum: A phenomenon in which a high-strength bolt, because of hydrogen that has entered the steel, suddenly fractures under a low load some time after being tightened. The higher the hardness, the greater the risk, so it is managed through the choice of plating or coating and the baking conditions.
facts: It occurs when three conditions overlap: high hardness (strength), tensile stress (including clamp load), and absorbed hydrogen.

Internal hydrogen embrittlement (IHE) is caused by hydrogen from manufacturing processes such as pickling, electroplating and phosphating, and environmental hydrogen embrittlement (EHE) by hydrogen generated in service by corrosion, cathodic protection or H2S.

ISO 4042 manages it by ISO 898-1 property class. No separate measure is needed for 9.8 or below; 10.9 requires process validation and product testing, or baking; and 12.9 requires both process validation and product testing, and baking.
RCSC (2025) considers that bolts above a tensile strength of 180 ksi (about 39 HRC) can become embrittled if hydrogen is present and they are under high tensile stress.

For hot-dip galvanizing, the problem is hydrogen from pickling. ISO 10684 requires parts of 320 HV or more to be cleaned by acid with inhibitor, alkaline or mechanical methods, and covers bolts only up to 10.9.
Zinc flake generates no hydrogen during application, so it is mainly used on high-strength bolts of 1000 MPa or more (ISO 10683).
Suspect lots are checked by a test in which the parts are held in the tightened state for a set time (such as ISO 15330).
watch: For electroplating of 10.9, 12.9, SAE Grade 8 and A574, state in the purchase order whether baking is done, its conditions, and the submission of records.
For grades whose standard limits the coating, such as F3125 A490, use only the permitted coatings (such as zinc flake).
High-strength bolts in a seawater cathodic protection zone can also fracture from hydrogen generated in service, so check the hardness upper limit in the specification.
Delayed fracture appears after time has passed, not immediately after tightening. Do not be reassured because nothing is wrong right after assembly.

t-baking.sum: A treatment in which parts are heated at a specified temperature for a specified time immediately after plating, to drive out the hydrogen that entered the steel during the plating process. It reduces the risk of hydrogen embrittlement in high-strength plated parts.
facts: Temperature and time are set by the process standard (ISO 9588, ASTM B850, etc.) and the order specification, according to part hardness, size and plating type.
ISO 4042 requires baking for 12.9 (specified maximum hardness above 390 HV), and allows 10.9 to be handled by process validation and product testing instead.
If baking is done on hot-dip galvanized parts, it is done before fluxing (surface activation) (ISO 10684).
Whether baking was done can be confirmed only if the plating certificate records the temperature, time and start time.
watch: For a quotation that says only "baking included", also check the temperature, time, the deadline for starting after plating, and whether records are submitted.
For 12.9 class, first consider another treatment that generates no hydrogen during application, such as zinc flake (ISO 10683).
If plating is stripped and redone, the parts go through pickling and plating again, so baking is also redone.

t-hdg.sum: A plating in which bolts and nuts are dipped in molten zinc and then spun off in a centrifuge, giving a thick zinc-iron alloy layer. Corrosion resistance is good, but the layer exceeds 40 µm, so the thread tolerance must be set separately and the nuts are overtapped.
facts: ISO 10684 is used for metric fasteners and ASTM F2329 for inch fasteners, and ASTM A153 is the general hot-dip zinc standard for iron and steel hardware. ISO 10684 covers M8 to M64 coarse threads, bolts up to 10.9 and nuts up to 12.
Hot-dip galvanizing is not recommended for threads under M8 or with a pitch under 1.25 mm.
The normal plating bath is 455 to 480 °C and high-temperature plating is 530 to 560 °C; for 10.9 M27 and above, high-temperature plating is not used, to prevent micro-cracks.

The layer always exceeds 40 µm, so the threads are fitted by one of two methods. Either the bolt is left standard (g·h) and the nut is tapped oversize after plating (6AZ·6AX), or the bolt is made undersize beforehand (6az) and the nut is tapped H·G after plating.
ISO 10684 requires parts of 320 HV or more to be cleaned by acid with inhibitor, alkaline or mechanical methods.
F3125 A490 is prohibited from hot-dip galvanizing (RCSC 2025), and 12.9 is outside the scope of ISO 10684 (bolts up to 10.9).
The thread tolerance cannot be checked by stripping the zinc after plating and applying a gauge, because part of the steel dissolves during plating.
watch: An ordinary nut will not go on a hot-dip galvanized bolt, and using an overtapped nut on an ordinary bolt gives too little thread engagement. Buy bolts and nuts as a set from the same process.
Do not use Z·X (overtapped) nuts together with U (undersize) bolts.
For 10.9 and above, A490, A354 BD, Grade 8 and A574, check before hot-dip galvanizing whether the standard permits it and how hydrogen embrittlement is controlled.
For A193 and A194 items, state the coating specification concretely in the purchase order.
Stacking while wet easily causes white rust, so specify a post-treatment (chromate or phosphate) if needed.
eq_notes: Hot-dip zinc for iron and steel hardware (fastener sampling follows F2329)
Hot-dip zinc for general steel fabrications (ISO 10684 for fasteners)

head: Method
Bolt (before plating)
Nut (tapped after plating)
Additional marking
rows: Z or X after the nut property class
table.note: Mixing Z·X nuts and U bolts carries a high risk of thread stripping. The 6AZ·6AX limits are in ISO 965-5, and 6az is in ISO 965-4.

t-overtap.sum: Tapping the nut larger than standard after plating, so that the thick coating on a hot-dip galvanized bolt fits. Thread engagement is reduced and assembly strength falls, so the method of pairing a nut of one property class higher is used.
facts: In ISO 10684, the nut (internal thread) is tapped after plating, and re-tapping is not permitted.
The tolerance is 6AZ or 6AX (ISO 965-5), and Z or X is stamped after the nut property class marking.
Because engagement is reduced, the nut threads may strip first. ISO 10684 Annex F (informative) deals with the strength of hot-dip galvanized bolt and nut assemblies.
For M8 and M10 overtapped nuts, the proof load is set separately, lower than the ISO 898-2 value.

For inch standards, ASTM A563 covers overtapping and grades of galvanized nuts. A325 galvanized sets use A563 DH nuts that are overtapped and lubricated, and the set undergoes a rotational capacity test.
In inch structural work, only hardened nuts that keep their strength after overtapping (A563 DH·DH3, A194 2H) are considered suitable as overtapped coated nuts (RCSC 2025).
Nuts mechanically galvanized (ASTM B695 Class 55) are also overtapped according to ASTM A563 (RCSC 2025).
watch: If an overtapped nut is used on an ungalvanized or electro-zinc bolt, engagement is insufficient and the threads may strip. Overtapped nuts are only for hot-dip galvanized bolts.
If the BOM has only "HDG nut" without a nut grade, check the mating bolt grade and the nut property class.
Do not re-tap on site because a plated nut will not go on. ISO 10684 does not permit re-tapping, so get a set again.
Hot-dip galvanizing of A490 is itself prohibited, so there is no overtapped nut combination either.

t-zinc-plating.sum: The most common bolt plating, in which a thin zinc layer is applied electrolytically and a conversion treatment adds color and corrosion resistance. For high-strength parts, look at hydrogen embrittlement, and for thickness, the thread tolerance.
facts: The references for fastener electroplating are ISO 4042 (zinc, zinc-nickel, zinc-iron, cadmium), ASTM F1941/F1941M for inch and metric fasteners, and ASTM B633 and ISO 2081 for general steel parts.

Color is determined by the conversion treatment (passivation), and there are white (blue-white), yellow, black and others. Hexavalent-chromium-free treatments (trivalent chromium, etc.) are now widely used in place of hexavalent chromium.
ASTM B633 divides thickness into four standard grades, and the current edition (2023) also provides hexavalent-chromium-free post-treatment types.

On a 60° thread, the effective diameter grows by about 4 times the plating thickness. An external thread with tolerance allowance such as 6g is plated within that allowance, while a 6h thread with no allowance has its pre-plating dimension reduced or another treatment is chosen.
ISO 4042: no additional hydrogen-related measure is needed for 9.8 or below; 10.9 requires process validation and product testing, or baking; and 12.9 requires both.
The friction coefficient differs with the conversion treatment, sealer and topcoat, so the clamp load changes even at the same torque.
watch: "YELLOW ZINC" and "colored chromate" on a drawing are notations that commonly meant a hexavalent chromium process, so for RoHS-regulated products, respecify with a hexavalent-chromium-free treatment.
Hexavalent and trivalent cannot be told apart by color alone. If needed, get a hexavalent chromium non-detection test result.
For high-hardness parts such as 10.9, 12.9, SAE Grade 8, A574 and spring washers, check the baking conditions or consider zinc flake.
If thick plating is required, the thread gauge may not go on even a 6g bolt. Specify thickness and thread tolerance together.

head: Color
Treatment
Remarks
rows: Formerly hexavalent chromate; now also trivalent treatments (including colored)
For 10.9 and above, check the baking conditions

t-zinc-flake.sum: A non-electrolytic coating made by applying a paint containing zinc and aluminum flakes and curing it by heating. No hydrogen is generated during application, so it is used as the corrosion-resistant coating for high-strength bolts such as 10.9, 12.9 and A490.
facts: The references are ISO 10683 (metric) and ASTM F3393 (inch, which replaced F1136, F2833 and F3019 in 2025), and it is used mainly to avoid internal hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength bolts of 1000 MPa or more.

If pretreatment is by alkaline or solvent cleaning followed by mechanical cleaning (blasting), no hydrogen is generated. Even where pickling is needed, parts above 390 HV or 12.9 and above are not pickled.

The curing temperature is up to about 320 °C depending on the system, and it must not exceed the tempering temperature of quenched and tempered parts. For bolts whose threads were rolled after heat treatment, the fatigue limit may be affected.
There are four configurations: basecoat only, basecoat + lubricant, basecoat + topcoat, and all three; the topcoat changes color, friction and chemical resistance.
The basic color is silver-gray, and black and others are produced with a topcoat.
There are both systems that contain hexavalent chromium and systems that do not, so decide which one when ordering.
It is a coating that can also be used on F3125 A490 (RCSC 2025: ASTM F3393 zinc flake permitted).
The corrosion resistance grade is set by the time without red rust in ISO 9227 neutral salt spray (240, 480, 600, 720, 960 h) (ISO 10683).
watch: The flake layer also takes up thread tolerance. A thick coat on standard bolts and nuts can cause gauge and assembly problems, so set an upper limit on thickness.
The friction coefficient differs with each coating and topcoat, so re-set the torque value according to the coating conditions.
On old drawings, a zinc flake designation with only a trade name does not show whether it contains hexavalent chromium. For RoHS-regulated products, respecify with a hexavalent-chromium-free system.
The required salt spray hours are not directly proportional to actual service life.
eq_notes: Inch zinc flake coating (replaced and consolidated F1136, F2833 and F3019 in 2025)

t-ptfe.sum: An organic coating of the fluoropolymer family applied to plant studs and nuts to give corrosion resistance and low friction. It is sometimes applied over a base layer (phosphate, zinc-based, etc.), and torque and thread fit differ from uncoated parts.
facts: Thickness, color, pretreatment and test items are usually set by the purchaser's specification or the coating product data, so state the coating specification concretely in the order.
The friction coefficient is low, so axial force is greater at the same torque. Use the torque value for the coating and tighten in stages.
Color (blue, green, black, etc.) differs by supplier and does not indicate grade or quality.
For ASTM bolting too, the coating specification is stated separately in the quotation and order. The manufacturer's certificate is usually the result for the condition before coating.
A coating cannot turn B7 into B7M, and does not replace the material requirements for sour-exposed bolting.
The upper service temperature differs for each coating product, so check it in the product datasheet.
watch: If the uncoated torque table is used as is, over-tightening may yield the stud or over-compress the gasket.
If the nut is tight because of the coating thickness, agree the thread fit (stud dimensions, nut tapping) with the coating supplier in advance.
Where the wrench has contacted and stripped the coating, only the base layer remains and rusts first. When reusing, check coating damage and thread condition.
Whether to apply another lubricant over a coated stud follows the conditions of the coating supplier's torque data.

t-black-oxide.sum: A treatment that chemically converts the steel surface into a black oxide film and impregnates it with rust-preventive oil or similar. Dimensional change is almost nil, but corrosion resistance is very limited, and for high-strength steel above 1000 MPa, take care about embrittlement during treatment.
facts: It is not plating but a conversion coating that changes the surface, so it is very thin and takes up almost none of the thread tolerance.
Corrosion resistance comes from the rust-preventive oil or wax on the coating, so it is for indoor and lubricated environments.
It is commonly used as the basic finish of socket head cap screws (socket head bolts).

ISO 11408 warns that high-strength steel above a tensile strength of 1000 MPa can crack from caustic embrittlement during the black oxide process, and requires hydrogen embrittlement relief heat treatment (ISO 9587·9588) before and after treatment if needed.
Examples of related standards: ISO 11408, MIL-DTL-13924.
watch: Outdoors and in damp places it rusts easily. If corrosion resistance is needed, choose zinc flake, zinc-nickel or stainless steel.
Black oxide and black zinc (black passivation) have similar names but very different corrosion resistance. State clearly in the order which one is meant.
If the rust-preventive oil is degreased before painting or bonding, rust forms quickly.
The rust-preventive oil changes friction, so match the lubrication conditions on which the torque is based.

t-phosphate.sum: A conversion coating that forms a zinc or manganese phosphate crystal layer on the steel surface and holds oil or wax. Its corrosion resistance alone is weak, but it is used as a base for lubrication and painting and for stable friction, and hydrogen can enter during treatment.
facts: Zinc phosphate is used as a base for painting and lubrication, and manganese phosphate, which holds oil well, is widely used to prevent wear and galling.
The color is gray to blackish gray, and it is often supplied as phosphate + rust-preventive oil.
It is an acid-solution process, so hydrogen can enter high-hardness parts, and a hydrogen removal treatment is done after treatment if needed.
ISO 10683 permits phosphate as pretreatment for zinc flake, because hydrogen escapes during flake curing.
The friction coefficient differs with the coating and oil condition, so the torque-clamp load relationship changes.
Examples of related standards: ISO 9717, MIL-DTL-16232.
watch: Phosphate + rust-preventive oil is not for long-term outdoor rust protection. If the oil dries out in storage, rust forms.
If phosphate is specified for high-hardness bolts and spring parts, check the hydrogen removal conditions.
Phosphate is sometimes used as the base for PTFE coating, so state the pretreatment in the coating specification.

t-cadmium.sum: A plating that was used on aerospace and marine bolts for its lubricity and salt-water corrosion resistance, but its use is greatly restricted by RoHS, ELV and similar regulations because of its toxicity. For general industrial use, the trend is to switch to zinc or zinc-nickel.
facts: EU RoHS does not allow cadmium to exceed 0.01 % (100 ppm) by weight of homogeneous material, a stricter limit than for the other restricted substances (0.1 %).

Cadmium use is restricted separately by the EU ELV Directive for automobiles and by REACH for chemicals in general. In Korea there is the Act on Resource Circulation of Electrical and Electronic Equipment and Vehicles.

The representative standards are ASTM B766 and ISO 2082 for cadmium electroplating and AMS-QQ-P-416 for aerospace, and ISO 4042, the standard for fastener electroplating, also covers cadmium. ASTM B696 for mechanical cadmium was withdrawn in 2026 without a replacement standard.
Cadmium fumes produced on heating, welding or cutting are highly toxic.
watch: "CAD PLATED" or "Cd" notations on old drawings and spare parts lists often have to be replaced with an alternative coating (zinc-nickel, etc.) and approved.
Bolts that go into export machinery and electrical products may be asked for a cadmium non-detection certificate.
Cadmium plating is similar in color to zinc plating and is hard to tell apart by eye. Confirm it by the certificate and the coating specification.

t-znni.sum: An electroplating of a zinc alloy mixed with nickel, with better corrosion resistance than zinc of the same thickness, used in place of plain zinc and cadmium for automotive, aerospace and plant bolting.
facts: For fasteners, it is one of the plating families covered by ISO 4042, and ASTM B841 is a zinc-nickel plating standard for general parts.
For alkaline zinc-nickel plating with 12 to 16 % nickel, ISO 4042 allows baking of high-strength parts to be omitted if the basis is confirmed by testing and the supplier and buyer agree.
It is used with a hexavalent-chromium-free passivation (or chromate) and a sealer, and finishes such as clear (silver) and black are available.
ISO 4042 notes that acid zinc-nickel has also been reported to have benefits similar to alkaline, but considers that more data is needed to decide on omitting baking.
As with electro-zinc, the thickness takes up thread tolerance, so thickness is set within the 6g allowance.
watch: Zinc-nickel is also electroplating. Omitting baking for 12.9 and high-hardness parts is accepted only when there is a test basis and agreement.
Writing only "zinc-nickel" does not set the nickel content, passivation, sealer or salt spray hours. State them together in the specification string.
When using it on high-temperature bolting, check the service temperature limit in the coating specification.

t-galling.sum: A phenomenon in which, when stainless steel or nickel alloy bolts and nuts are tightened, the thin oxide film on the thread surfaces breaks and the metals stick together. Once it occurs, the fastener can be neither tightened further nor loosened, and the bolt breaks easily.
facts: It commonly occurs on austenitic stainless steel (304, 316, A2, A4, B8, B8M) bolts and nuts.
The risk increases with the same material on both parts, fast tightening (impact or power tools), high load, rough thread surfaces or foreign matter, and no lubrication.
Countermeasures are anti-seize compound, slow tightening, clean thread surfaces, a difference in hardness or material between bolt and nut, and lubricating finishes such as wax or dry film.
Galling countermeasures are often managed through order and installation conditions rather than product standards.
Even at the same torque, the clamp load differs greatly depending on the lubricant, so match the lubrication conditions of the torque table.
watch: If stainless steel bolts are tightened quickly with an impact wrench, galling occurs easily. Tighten with hand tools or at low speed.
A galled bolt may break if forcibly loosened, so allow a margin in the replacement quantity.
If anti-seize compound is applied, the torque must be reduced. Using the dry-condition torque as is leads to over-tightening.
Where lubricants are restricted, such as oxygen equipment, first check the permitted lubricants.

t-galvanic.sum: A phenomenon in which, when two metals of different potential touch in an electrolyte such as water or seawater, the less noble one corrodes faster. Because a bolt has a small area, the rule is to use a material equal to or nobler than the mating member.
facts: There are three conditions: two metals of different potential, electrical contact, and an electrolyte connecting them. If one is broken, corrosion stops or decreases.
A small anode + a large cathode is the worst case. If a stainless steel plate is fastened with carbon steel or galvanized bolts, the bolts rust quickly.

Conversely, if carbon steel members are fastened with stainless steel bolts, the bolt is protected and the increase in corrosion on the large member side is relatively small. However, in seawater corrosion around the hole can occur, so insulating washers and sealant are used.
Zinc plating works on this principle, where the zinc dissolves first and protects the steel (sacrificial mode).
The potential order of metals in seawater (galvanic series) is judged by guides such as ASTM G82.
watch: In seawater and cooling water equipment, if the bolt is made of a less noble material than the member (for example, fastening a stainless steel member with carbon steel bolts), the bolt rusts first. Select the same family as the member or nobler.
An insulating flange kit (sleeves, washers, gasket) is meant to break the electrical contact between the bolt and the flange. If a sleeve is missing or cracked, the insulation fails.
For high-strength bolts in a cathodic protection zone, hydrogen embrittlement rather than corrosion can be the problem.
Graphite gaskets and graphite-containing lubricants have a high potential and, in wet environments, can increase corrosion on the steel or stainless steel side.

t-scc.sum: A phenomenon in which tensile stress and a specific corrosive environment act together on a susceptible material, and branched cracks grow even under low load. For bolts, the clamp load itself is a large tensile stress, so choosing a material suited to the environment is important.
facts: It occurs when three things overlap: a susceptible material, tensile stress and a specific environment, and clamp load and residual stress are included in the tensile stress.
Austenitic stainless steel (304, 316, B8, B8M, A2, A4) is prone to chloride SCC in warm chloride environments. Typical cases are wet piping under insulation and coastal atmosphere.
Duplex and super duplex steels and alloys with high nickel content resist chloride SCC better than austenitic steels, and are used for bolting on seawater and chloride equipment.
For high-strength carbon and low-alloy steels, the problems are sulfide stress cracking (SSC) in H2S environments and cracking from hydrogen in service, and these are managed by hardness limits.
SCC is known for copper alloys such as brass in ammonia, and for carbon steel in concentrated caustic soda.
watch: For stainless steel bolting wrapped with insulation, watch for chlorides leaching out of the insulation.
Do not use 304 or 316 bolts in high-temperature seawater and chloride equipment on the judgment that "stainless steel does not rust".
Over-tightening well beyond the design clamp load increases the SCC risk.

t-passivation.sum: A treatment that dissolves free iron (iron picked up from processing and tools) and contamination from the stainless steel surface with acid and lets the chromium oxide film form evenly. It is not a coating, and color and dimensions hardly change.
facts: The representative standards are ISO 16048 for fastener passivation, and ASTM A967 (chemical passivation) and ASTM A380 (cleaning, descaling and passivation) for general stainless steel parts.
There are nitric acid-based and citric acid-based treatments, and after treatment it is checked by water immersion, humidity, salt spray, copper sulfate tests and so on that no free iron remains.
Pickling is a stronger treatment that also removes heat treatment and welding scale, while passivation finishes a scale-free surface.

For martensitic and precipitation-hardening grades (410, 630, etc.), treatment conditions suited to the material must be chosen. ASTM A967 provides an appendix with guidance on selecting the treatment by steel type.
Passivation does not change the corrosion limits of the material. Treating 304 does not make it 316 or duplex for seawater.
watch: A "passivation treatment" requirement is meaningful only if the applicable standard (ISO 16048, A967, etc.) and the verification test are stated together.
If stainless steel bolts are handled with iron tools or wire brushes, iron particles stick and rust spots form.
To tell whether spot rust on a stainless steel bolt is a material problem or surface contamination, look at the surface treatment condition together with the composition.

t-rohs.sum: EU RoHS sets maximum concentrations of 10 substances, including hexavalent chromium, lead and cadmium, in homogeneous materials of electrical and electronic products. For bolts, the main issues are chromate plating, cadmium, and lead-containing free-machining material.
facts: The limit concentration is 0.1 % by weight of homogeneous material (hexavalent chromium, lead, mercury, PBB, PBDE, and four phthalates), and only cadmium is 0.01 %.

Hexavalent chromium in fastener plating is found in traditional chromate conversion coatings and in zinc flake containing hexavalent chromium. These are now being replaced with hexavalent-chromium-free passivation and flake.
Automobiles are restricted separately by the EU ELV Directive and chemicals in general by REACH. In Korea there is the Act on Resource Circulation of Electrical and Electronic Equipment and Vehicles.
Tests used to check hexavalent chromium in plating coatings include IEC 62321-7-1 (colorimetric method for colorless and colored conversion coatings).
Some uses, such as lead-containing free-machining steel and brass, have RoHS exemption clauses, but the scope and expiry of exemptions are revised, so check the current list.

RoHS obligations lie with manufacturers, importers and others who place electrical and electronic products on the market, so fastener suppliers usually back this up with a non-detection test certificate or a declaration of conformity.
watch: "YELLOW ZINC" and "ZINC CHROMATE" in drawings and BOMs may be notations that meant hexavalent chromate. For a regulated product, state "trivalent" or "Cr(VI)-free" explicitly.
It cannot be concluded that yellow means hexavalent and silver means trivalent. If needed, get a test result.
RoHS compliance looks not only at the plating but also at the bolt body material (lead-containing free-machining material, etc.).

t-anti-seize.sum: A solid lubricant paste applied at high-temperature, corroding and stainless steel fastening points so that the threads do not seize and can be loosened later. It changes the friction coefficient greatly, so the torque value must always be set on the basis of that lubricant.
facts: There are metal powder types such as copper and nickel, graphite types, and molybdenum disulfide (MoS2) types, and the service temperature and material compatibility differ for each.
The torque needed for the same clamp load varies greatly with the lubricant. The lubrication condition of the torque table or K value (nut factor) must be the same as the actual lubricant.
Apply it to both the threaded portion and the nut bearing face. Bearing face friction also accounts for a large share of the tightening torque.
For oxygen equipment, do not use hydrocarbon-based lubricants; use only lubricants permitted for oxygen.
For stainless steel and nickel alloy high-temperature parts, products with limited halogen and sulfur content are sometimes specified (to prevent stress corrosion and high-temperature corrosion).
watch: If a bolt with anti-seize compound is tightened using a dry (unlubricated) torque table, over-tightening may yield the stud or over-compress the gasket.
Copper-based compounds are not used where copper must be avoided, such as acetylene and ammonia equipment.
Whether to apply a lubricant over a PTFE-coated stud follows the conditions of the coating supplier's torque data.
For sour and high-temperature equipment, the specification sometimes designates the lubricant type, so check first.

t-salt-spray.sum: An accelerated test in which an approximately 5 % sodium chloride solution is sprayed as a mist in a test chamber to compare the relative corrosion resistance of coatings. "480 h" in a coating specification means no rust may be visible during that time.
facts: Neutral salt spray (NSS) is represented by ISO 9227 and ASTM B117, and ISO 9227 uses an approximately 5 % sodium chloride solution. ISO 9227 also has acetic acid salt spray (AASS) and copper-accelerated acetic acid salt spray (CASS).
For zinc-family coatings, the times to white rust (zinc corrosion product) and to red rust (base steel corrosion) are looked at separately.
For zinc flake (ISO 10683), grades (240 to 960 h) are set on the criterion of no red rust for the specified time.
Accelerated test time is not directly proportional to actual service life. Use it as a tool for comparing coatings.
Some specifications also require cyclic corrosion tests (repeated salt, drying and wetting) that are closer to the real environment.
watch: If only "salt spray 480 hours" is written without saying white rust or red rust, the judgment can differ.

ISO 10683 has the parts tested 24 hours after coating, in the condition before sorting and packing. Delivered goods that have gone through transport and automatic sorting may have lower corrosion resistance than the test result.
The test result is a value for the parts tested. If a test on the delivered lot is needed, specify it separately when ordering.

t-mech-zinc.sum: A plating in which parts are tumbled in a drum with glass beads, zinc powder and chemicals, and zinc is peened onto them at room temperature. No electricity is used and thick layers are possible, so it is used as an alternative to hot-dip galvanizing for structural bolts and anchors.
facts: ASTM B695 divides thickness into several Classes, and the thickest Class is 107 µm. The seven thick Classes are commonly called "mechanical zinc plating", and Class 55 is specified for structural bolts and nuts.
ASTM F3125 A325 permits hot-dip galvanizing (F2329) or B695 Class 55 as the zinc coating, and neither is permitted for A490 (RCSC 2025).
Bolts and nuts are matched by the same zinc process (hot-dip with hot-dip, mechanical with mechanical), and mechanically zinc-coated nuts are also overtapped according to ASTM A563 (RCSC 2025).

It is a room-temperature process, so there is no heat effect from a high-temperature plating bath. Hydrogen that can enter in pretreatment such as acid cleaning is checked separately for high-strength parts.
watch: Do not mix hot-dip galvanized bolts with mechanically zinc-coated nuts.
For Class 55 sets, get a set from the same process using nuts overtapped according to ASTM A563.
For high-strength parts of A490 and 10.9 or above, first check the permitted coatings in the standard.

t-unc-unf.sum: The 60° inch threads of ASME B1.1. UNC is the coarse pitch set for each diameter and UNF the fine pitch, and the size is written by threads per inch (TPI). Below 1/4", numbered designations such as #10 are used.
facts: An inch thread with a 60° thread angle; ISO also has the same series as ISO inch screw threads (ISO 263). Diameter is written in fractional inches and pitch in TPI (threads per inch), and the pitches differ from metric threads, so the two do not fit each other.
Below 1/4", numbered designations are used: #4-40, #6-32, #8-32, #10-24 (UNC) · #10-32 (UNF). #10 has a diameter of 0.190" (4.83 mm).

For UNC, the pitch gets coarser as the diameter grows (1-1/2" 6 threads, 2" 4-1/2 threads), so the loss of stress area on large bolts is greater. 8UN (fixed 8 threads per inch) is widely used instead of UNC at diameters above 1" (NIST H28).
In addition there are UNEF (extra fine series) and the constant-pitch series (4UN·6UN·8UN·12UN·16UN·20UN·28UN·32UN).
Thread series of the old American National designation such as NC and NF have been replaced by the UN series (NIST H28).
watch: If the BOM has no TPI, as in "1/2" bolt", ask whether it is UNC or UNF. UNC is for mass production of general bolts and nuts, and UNF is used where coarse threads do not fit, such as short engagement and thin walls (NIST H28).

For a BOM that lists a high-temperature, high-pressure flange stud above 1" as UNC (for example, 1-1/8"-7 UNC), confirm whether 8UN is correct. NIST H28 recommends the 8-thread series above 1" for such bolting.

t-8un.sum: A Unified constant-pitch series with 8 threads per inch (pitch 3.175 mm) regardless of diameter. It is widely used instead of UNC at diameters above 1", and for high-temperature, high-strength bolting, UNC at 1" and below and 8UN above 1" are recommended (NIST H28).
facts: 8UN is one of the constant-pitch series of ASME B1.1, and the TPI stays fixed at 8 even as the diameter changes (pitch 25.4/8 = 3.175 mm).

NIST H28 (3.7) recommends UNC for 0.25 to 1" and the 8-thread series above 1" for high-temperature, high-strength bolting. The ORNL report (1976) commissioned by the US NRC, which evaluated B16.5 flange bolting, also used UNC at 1" and below and 8 threads at 1-1/8" and above.
The 8 threads at 1" are a standard size of the UNC series, so it is written "1"-8 UNC" (ISO 2306, NIST H28). So the difference between UNC and 8UN begins at 1-1/8" (UNC 7 threads vs 8UN 8 threads).
At the same diameter the stress area is larger than UNC: 1-1/8" is 0.790 in² (8UN) vs 0.763 in² (UNC), and 1-1/2" is 1.492 in² vs 1.405 in² (about 6%).
watch: If the flange BOM has only "1-1/8" stud" and no TPI, confirm whether it is UNC with 7 threads or 8UN with 8 threads. For high-temperature, high-pressure bolting, 8UN above 1" is recommended (NIST H28).
When changing only the nuts, check the thread series (TPI) so that UNC nuts are not mixed with 8UN studs.
Tap-end studs and casing bolts follow the equipment drawing, not the flange rules. They may be UNC even above 1".

t-unr.sum: UNR is a UN external thread with a rounded root and fits ordinary UN internal threads (there is no UNR internal thread). UNJ is a high-fatigue form in which the external thread root radius is enlarged to 0.150P–0.180P; it was in B1.15 and was consolidated into ASME B1.1-2019.
facts: UNR is a designation used only for external threads. Apart from the rounded root it is the same as UN, so a UNRC external thread fits a UNC internal thread (2B) as is.

UNJ is a form in which the external thread root radius is enlarged to 0.150P–0.180P. Stress concentration at the root is reduced, so it is used for high-strength, high-fatigue parts. UNJ, which was in ASME B1.15, was consolidated into B1.1-2019.
ASME B1.1 (2024) shows with a figure an example in which a maximum-material UNJ-3A external thread and a UN-3B internal thread interfere on assembly.
The metric equivalent is the aerospace MJ thread (ISO 5855).
watch: Buying UNC or UNF in place of UNRC or UNRF on a drawing will still assemble, but if the designation was made with fatigue in mind (connecting rods, couplings, socket head cap screws), the rounded root requirement is lost. Receive it as specified.
If a nut or tapped hole specification reads "UNR-2B", it is a mistake. UNR is for external threads only, so confirm with UNC-2B or similar.
If a UNJ (aerospace) bolt is replaced with a UN bolt, the basis for fatigue strength is lost. Conversely, a UNJ external thread may not go into an ordinary UN internal thread.
eq_notes: Former standard of the UNJ thread (consolidated into ASME B1.1-2019)

t-inch-class.sum: A is the external thread and B the internal thread, and the larger the number, the tighter the tolerance. General bolts and nuts are 2A/2B and precision parts 3A/3B. Only 1A and 2A external threads have a clearance (allowance) from the basic size.
facts: The classes are set in ASME B1.1. External threads are 1A·2A·3A and internal threads 1B·2B·3B. Any internal thread class assembles with any external thread class.
The allowance (the clearance by which the part is made smaller than the basic size) exists only for 1A and 2A (the same value for both classes), and is 0 for 3A and all B classes.

Example: the maximum major diameter of 3/4"-10 UNC-2A is 0.7482", which is smaller than the basic 0.750" by the allowance of 0.0018" (allowance = 0.3 × the 2A pitch diameter tolerance). The maximum major diameter of 3A is the basic size, 0.7500".
2A/2B is the class most widely used for general fasteners such as bolts and nuts. 2A/2B is also recommended for high-temperature, high-pressure pressure vessel and pipe flange bolting (NIST H28).
3A/3B is the precision class used where fit accuracy and lead and angle accuracy matter (NIST H28).
1A/1B is a class with a widened tolerance for easy assembly and is rare outside special uses.

The 2A allowance can be used as plating allowance, so the 2A maximum size applies to the part before plating and the basic size to the part after plating. The 1A allowance is not for plating (NIST H28). For thick coatings such as hot-dip galvanizing, the nut is overtapped (RCSC 2025 commentary).
watch: A BOM with only "3/4-10 UNC" and no class is usually taken as 2A/2B (the standard class for general fasteners, NIST H28). If the part needs a precision fit (3A), check the drawing.
An ordinary (2B) nut will not go on a hot-dip galvanized bolt as is. Pair it with an overtapped nut.
A common error is writing "-2B" in a bolt specification and "-2A" in a nut specification. A = external thread, B = internal thread.
Inch 2A and metric 6g play a similar role (general class), but the numerical systems differ and they cannot be written in place of each other.

t-inch-designation.t: Reading an inch thread designation (3/4"-10 UNC-2A)
t-inch-designation.sum: "3/4"-10 UNC-2A" means a nominal diameter of 3/4" (19.05 mm), 10 threads per inch, the UNC series, and class 2A external thread. Right-hand is the default, and only left-hand has LH added at the end.
facts: Order: nominal diameter - TPI series-class (direction). Examples: 7/8"-9 UNC-2A, 1-1/4"-8UN-2B, #10-32 UNF-3A.
The diameter is written in fractional inches (3/4") or decimals (0.750). The hyphen in "1-1/4" joins 1 and 1/4, and 1-1/4" = 1.25" = 31.75 mm.
With two hyphens, as in "1-1/4-8", the first part is the diameter (1-1/4") and the second is the TPI (8).
External thread is A and internal thread is B. Right-hand is not marked, and only left-hand has LH added (example: 3/4"-10 UNC-2A-LH).
NC and NF on old drawings (American designations before unification) are read as UNC and UNF of the same diameter and TPI.
watch: For a BOM with "3/4" × 4"" and no TPI, confirm whether it is UNC (10 threads) or UNF (16 threads). Above 1", UNC and 8UN also diverge (1-1/8"-7 UNC vs 1-1/8"-8UN).
"1 1/4", "1.1/4" and "1-1/4" are all 1.25". Conversely, "1-1/4-7" is sometimes misread as "1-1/4" length 7"".
Do not confuse #10 (numbered thread, diameter 0.190" = 4.83 mm) with M10.
Correct an error such as 2B on a bolt and 2A on a nut with the rule A = external thread, B = internal thread, and confirm it.

t-metric-coarse-fine.sum: For each diameter, a metric thread has one coarse pitch and several fine pitches set. A coarse thread omits the pitch and is written M16, and a fine thread must always give the pitch, as in M16×1.5.
facts: The basic thread form is ISO 68-1 (60°), the diameter and pitch combinations are ISO 261, and the selection for bolts and nuts is ISO 262. In KS, they are KS B 0201 (coarse) and KS B 0204 (fine).
At the same diameter a fine thread has a slightly larger stress area: M16×2 157 mm² vs M16×1.5 167 mm², M20×2.5 245 mm² vs M20×1.5 272 mm².

Fine threads are advantageous for fine adjustment, thin walls, and nuts at shaft ends (such as bearing lock nuts). On the other hand, the threads are shallow, so they are sensitive to damage, galling and plating thickness, and are at a disadvantage against stripping in soft internal threads.
Product standards for fine-thread hex products: bolts ISO 8765 (partially threaded) and ISO 8676 (fully threaded), nuts ISO 8673.
watch: If the drawing is for a fine thread but the BOM has only "M16", it will be interpreted as coarse (×2). Copy the pitch from the drawing into the BOM.
ISO 262 fine pitches include designations with two, such as M10 (1.25·1), M12 (1.5·1.25) and M18 to M22 (2·1.5), so the pitch must be checked too.
A pitch of 1.5 mm and 16 TPI (1.5875 mm) are hard to tell apart over a short length. Do not decide with a single pitch gauge; measure the diameter too.
Fine threads also have smaller tolerance clearance, so nuts failing to go on plated parts happens more often.

t-metric-tol.sum: A metric thread tolerance is written with a number (tolerance width) and a letter (position). Lowercase is an external thread and uppercase an internal thread. General bolts and nuts use 6g/6H, and nuts for hot-dip galvanized bolts use the overtapped 6AZ·6AX.
facts: In "6g", 6 is the tolerance grade (width) and g is the tolerance position (how far it is from the basic size). External thread positions are a to g (negative fundamental deviation) and h (0), and internal threads are G (positive) and H (0) (ISO 965-1).
The basic for general fasteners is bolt 6g and nut 6H (ISO 965-1). Product grade C bolts are 8g (6g for strength 8.8 and above) and C nuts are 7H, which is coarser (ISO 4759-1, ISO 4034).
The clearance at position g (fundamental deviation) grows as the pitch grows. The 6g of M16×2 starts 0.038 mm smaller than the basic size (fundamental deviation −38 µm).

On a 60° thread, a plating thickness t increases the pitch diameter by about 4t. So electroplating must fit within the g clearance, and thick coatings use positions with large clearance such as e and f.

There are two ways to fit hot-dip galvanized (HDG) pairs (ISO 10684). (1) The bolt is made to position g or h before plating and plated, and the nut is overtapped to 6AZ·6AX after plating (nut marking Z·X). (2) The bolt is made small as 6az before plating (bolt marking U), and the nut is tapped to H or G after plating.

6AZ has a small fundamental deviation and is for bolts with thin plating, and 6AX is for bolts with thick plating. Fundamental deviation AZ +(300 + 20P) µm, AX +(220P − 20) µm (ISO 965-5, AX is for pitch 1.75 mm and above). At M16, AZ is +0.34 mm and AX is +0.42 mm.

An overtapped nut has shallower engagement and so loses strength. ISO 10684 sets the proof load of M8 and M10 overtapped nuts separately, lower than ISO 898-2 (Annex A), and for inch structural bolting only hardened nuts (A563 DH·DH3, A194 2H) are used as galvanized nuts (RCSC 2025 commentary).
watch: If an overtapped nut (Z·X) is paired with an undersize bolt (U), clearance arises twice over and the risk of thread stripping is high. Do not mix the two methods.
If only hot-dip galvanized bolts are bought and the nuts are bought as ordinary 6H, they will not go on. Receive hot-dip galvanized bolts and nuts as a set fitted by the same method.
"6H/6g" is the nut/bolt pair designation. If the drawing has no tolerance, the general class (6H/6g) is assumed.
If an electroplated bolt is inspected with the pre-plating reference gauge, it may be rejected. Decide the inspection point (before or after plating).

t-metric-designation.sum: "M16×2-6g" means an ISO metric thread, nominal diameter 16 mm, pitch 2 mm, and external thread tolerance 6g. The pitch can be omitted for a coarse thread but must always be written for a fine thread.
facts: M = ISO metric thread (60°), number = nominal diameter (mm), after × = pitch (mm), after - = tolerance class, and LH attached with a dash at the end = left-hand thread.
A coarse thread is written M16 and a fine thread M16×1.5. Writing the coarse pitch as in "M16×2" is not wrong either.

The tolerance is lowercase for external threads (6g) and uppercase for internal threads (6H), and the pair is 6H/6g. If there is no tolerance designation, the medium class 6H/6g (M1.6 and above) is assumed (ISO 965-1).
For multi-start threads, the lead and pitch are written together: M16×Ph3P1.5-6H (lead 3, pitch 1.5, 2 starts). The number of starts is sometimes added in parentheses (ISO 965-1).
The product designation is in the order of product name, standard, thread × length, and property class: hex bolt ISO 4014 - M12 × 80 - 8.8.
The KS for thread designation is KS B 0200 (designation of screw threads).
watch: If "M16" on a fine-thread drawing is carried into the BOM without a pitch, M16×2 will arrive. Check the pitch in the drawing title block or thread table.
"M16x2.0", "M16-2.0" and "M16 P2" are all M16×2. Conversely, "M16-1.5" is a fine thread.
M10×1.25 and M10×1, and M12×1.25 and M12×1.5, do not fit each other. Check the pitch of the existing part.
M16 and inch 5/8" (15.88 mm) differ in both diameter and pitch and cannot replace each other.

t-tpi-pitch.sum: Pitch (mm) = 25.4 / TPI. 3/4"-10 UNC has a pitch of 2.540 mm and 1"-8 has 3.175 mm. Many values are close to metric pitches, so deciding with a single pitch gauge easily goes wrong.
facts: P (mm) = 25.4 / TPI, TPI = 25.4 / P. Examples: 13 TPI → 1.954 mm, pitch 1.5 mm → 16.93 TPI.
Inch threads are written by TPI and metric threads by pitch (mm). For multi-start threads, lead (travel per turn) = pitch × number of starts.
Pairs with a small difference, such as 10 TPI (2.540 mm) and 2.5 mm, 16 TPI (1.5875 mm) and 1.5 mm, and 20 TPI (1.270 mm) and 1.25 mm, are hard to tell apart by gauge over a short length.
Decide with a pitch gauge + outside diameter measurement + matching ring and plug gauges.
watch: Check whether "pitch 1.5" in the BOM is metric, or a rounding of 16 TPI from an inch drawing.
Distinguish heavy nuts for 3/4" bolts from M20 nuts by the markings and the width across flats (3/4" heavy nut 1-1/4" = 31.75 mm, M20 ISO nut 30 mm).
Apply the pitch gauge over as long a length as possible, not just a few threads.

t-left-hand.sum: A thread that is tightened by turning counterclockwise. LH is added at the end of the designation (M16×1.5-LH, 3/4"-10 UNC-2A-LH). Right-hand is the default, so if LH is missing it is read as right-hand.
facts: Designation: metric M16×1.5-LH, inch 3/4"-10 UNC-2A-LH. Right-hand is not marked (ISO 965-1, NIST H28).

Uses: nuts at shaft ends where the direction of rotation could loosen a right-hand thread (such as the left wheel of a bench grinder), one end of a turnbuckle where both sides are pulled together, and some gas connections where wrong assembly must be prevented.
For parts whose LH or RH depends on the direction of rotation, such as pump and blower impeller nuts, it differs from machine to machine.
watch: If LH is missing from the BOM, it is interpreted as right-hand. For a replacement part, first check the thread direction of the actual part.
Turnbuckles and connecting rods have different directions at the two ends. When ordering only one, state which end.
Left-hand threads need separate taps, dies and gauges and are often made to order. Fix the specification (thread direction, class) early.
If LH is not written in a disassembly work instruction, force is applied the wrong way and the threads or tools are damaged.

t-stress-area.sum: The cross-sectional area used when calculating the tensile strength of the threaded portion. For inch, As = 0.7854(D − 0.9743/n)² in², and for metric, As = 0.7854(d − 0.9382P)² mm². It is the basis for proof load and preload stress calculations.
facts: Inch (NIST H28 Appendix A5): As = 0.7854 × (D − 0.9743/n)² [in²], D = nominal diameter (in), n = TPI.

Example: the 3/4" shank is 0.442 in² vs As 0.334 in² (about 24% smaller), and the M16 shank is 201 mm² vs As 157 mm² (about 22% smaller). The smaller the diameter and the coarser the pitch, the larger the difference (1/4"-20 is about 35%).
Proof load = As × proof stress, minimum breaking load = As × minimum tensile strength, bolt stress = preload / As.
Pressure vessel flange design (ASME BPVC Section VIII Div.1 Appendix 2) uses the root area, not As. Even for the same bolt, the area basis may differ from one calculation to another.
watch: Check whether the load calculation used the stress area, the root area or the shank area. Torque tables also give different values if the reference area differs.
Changing UNC to 8UN increases As (from 0.763 to 0.790 in² at 1-1/8"). Even for the same stress target, use torque and preload tables that match the thread series.
For reduced-shank (waisted) bolts, the shank may be smaller than As, so judge by the minimum cross-section.

t-proof-load.sum: The test load that must leave no permanent deformation when applied to and removed from a bolt or nut. For a bolt it is As × proof stress, about 10% lower than the yield strength. The proof load of M16 8.8 is about 91 kN.
facts: Bolt proof load = As × proof stress (Sp) (ISO 898-1 Table 5). The test methods are in the finished-product proof load test of ISO 898-1 and in ASTM F606.
ISO 898-1 proof stress: 8.8 580 MPa (d ≤ 16 mm) · 600 MPa (d > 16 mm), 10.9 830 MPa, 12.9 970 MPa. This is about 88 to 91% of the yield strength.
watch: Proof load is not the yield load. "Proof load: OK" on a certificate means there was no permanent elongation at that load; it is not a yield value.

Overtapped hot-dip galvanized nuts have reduced engagement and lower strength. For structural use, only hardened nuts (A563 DH·DH3, A194 2H) are used as galvanized nuts (RCSC 2025 commentary), and ISO 10684 sets the proof load of M8 and M10 overtapped nuts separately, lower.
If only the property class is matched and the diameter range is missed (for example, the 16 mm boundary of 8.8), the value is wrong.

t-yield-tensile.sum: Tensile strength (Rm) is the maximum stress before breaking, and yield strength (ReL·Rp0.2) is the stress at which permanent deformation begins. 8.8 means a nominal Rm of 800 MPa and a yield of 0.8 × 800 = 640 MPa.
facts: Tensile strength Rm = maximum load ÷ cross-sectional area (As for an actual bolt). Yield strength is ReL if there is a distinct yield point, and otherwise the stress at 0.2% permanent elongation, Rp0.2 (0.2% offset in inch standards).
For property class "8.8": the first number × 100 = nominal tensile strength (MPa), and the second number × 10 = yield ratio (%). 10.9 → nominal 1,000 MPa, yield 900 MPa.
Nominal and minimum differ: 10.9 has a minimum Rm of 1,040 and Rp0.2 of 940 MPa, and 8.8 at d > 16 mm has Rm 830 and Rp0.2 660 MPa.
The "70" in stainless steel A2-70 and A4-70 means a minimum tensile strength of 700 MPa, and the "80" in A2-80 and A4-80 means 800 MPa (ISO 3506-1).
Full-size testing (the whole bolt is pulled; for bolts with heads, a wedge test) and test piece testing (a specimen machined from bar) can give different values.
Units: 1 ksi = 6.895 MPa. Examples: 125 ksi = 862 MPa, 105 ksi = 724 MPa.
watch: Do not design with the nominal value of the class number; use the standard minimum value and the diameter range (for example, the 16 mm boundary of 8.8).
The higher the strength, the more sensitive to hydrogen embrittlement and delayed fracture. For electroplated 10.9 and 12.9, check measures such as baking.
Inch-edition (ksi) and SI-edition (MPa) standards set their values separately, so a converted ksi value may differ from the SI-edition value. Check which edition the certificate is based on.

t-preload.sum: The tensile force produced in the bolt by tightening, which is also the force pressing the clamped parts together. It keeps the joint faces from separating or slipping when an external load arrives, and reduces the cyclic load the bolt sees.
facts: Preload F creates tension in the bolt and compression of the same size in the clamped parts (flange, gasket). The joint faces stay together until an external load has relieved all of this compression.

Of an external load P, the share the bolt additionally carries is Φ·P, with Φ ≈ kb / (kb + kc) (kb bolt stiffness, kc clamped part stiffness). The longer and more slender the bolt, the smaller Φ is, which is favorable for fatigue.
Bolt elongation δ = F·L / (E·A). In steel (E ≈ 205 GPa), a stress of 345 MPa (50 ksi) stretches it about 0.17 mm per 100 mm of length.
Structural high-strength bolts (RCSC) are given 70% of the minimum tensile strength as preload: 3/4" A325 → 0.70 × 120 ksi × 0.334 in² ≈ 28 kip, A490 ≈ 35 kip.
Preload decreases over time: embedment (settlement) of contact surfaces, gasket creep and relaxation, temperature change, and elastic interaction of neighboring bolts during tightening.
Methods of producing preload: torque, nut rotation angle, hydraulic tensioning, elongation measurement (micrometer, ultrasonic), direct tension indicator washers (DTI), TC bolts.
watch: Do not accept only "torque in N·m"; also get the target preload (or bolt stress) and the lubrication condition. Torque is only a means of producing preload.
If the washer, coating or lubricant is changed, the preload at the same torque changes greatly.
Gasketed joints relax a great deal after the first tightening. Include in the procedure whether retightening (a circular pass after a set time) is done.
The bolt stress in a pressure vessel calculation may be based on the root area. Do not mix it with a preload table based on the stress area.

t-torque.t: Tightening torque and the K factor
t-torque.sum: The relation between torque and preload is commonly approximated as T = K·D·F. K (nut factor) is an empirical value that lumps together thread and bearing face friction, so if the lubrication or coating changes, the preload at the same torque changes greatly.
facts: Simple formula: T = K × D × F. In SI, T [N·m] = K × d [m] × F [N], and in inch, T [lbf·ft] = K × D [in] × F [lbf] / 12.

Detailed formula (ISO 16047, VDI 2230 family): T = F × (P/2π + 0.577·μth·d2 + μb·Db/2). It is the sum of the pitch term, the thread friction term and the bearing face friction term (d2 pitch diameter, Db mean bearing face diameter).
Most of the torque is used up by friction. It is commonly explained as about 50% bearing face friction, about 40% thread friction, and about 10% for stretching the bolt.

K is commonly assumed to be 0.2, but it should not be used as is. NASA RP-1228 gives 0.15 as a more realistic typical value for steel on steel. It varies greatly with lubricant and coating, so the actual value is set from the manufacturer's data or by testing.
Units: 1 lbf·ft = 1.356 N·m, 1 kgf·m = 9.807 N·m, 1 lbf = 4.448 N.
watch: The K (or μ) of the torque table must be the same as the lubrication condition in the field. If anti-seize compound is applied and unlubricated torque is used, the result is over-tightening (bolt yielding, gasket over-compression).

Studs with PTFE coating or zinc flake coating with a lubricating topcoat have low friction, so preload is greater at the same torque. Use the torque value for the coating condition (the same intent as the warning in the site's flange calculator).
Confusion of torque units (ft·lb, in·lb, N·m, kgf·m) is frequent. State the unit together in the procedure.
Normally the nut side is turned. If the bolt head is turned, shank twist and friction conditions differ and the preload differs at the same torque, so set the torque for that condition separately.
The presence of a hardened washer and the bearing face roughness also change K. If the washer is removed or changed, set the torque again.

t-torque-scatter.t: Clamp load scatter in torque tightening
t-torque-scatter.sum: Even when tightened to the same torque, friction differs from bolt to bolt, so preload commonly scatters by around ±25%. The design must withstand both the minimum preload (leakage, slip) and the maximum preload (yield, gasket crushing).
facts: About 90% of the torque is used by friction, so even a small change in the friction coefficient changes the preload greatly. Friction scatter is far larger than the error of a calibrated torque wrench (a few %).
When there is no data, NASA-STD-5020 takes the preload variation of torque tightening as ±25% lubricated and ±35% unlubricated. At ±25%, the ratio of maximum to minimum preload is 1.25 / 0.75 ≈ 1.7.
Causes of scatter: lubricant type and amount, coating, thread and bearing face roughness, reuse, tightening speed, hole perpendicularity, washer hardness.
Control precision generally improves in the order torque < nut rotation angle < hydraulic tensioning or direct tension indicator washers < bolt elongation measurement (ultrasonic, etc.).
A flange is tightened bolt by bolt in sequence, so elastic interaction (the bolt tightened first being loosened) is added. That is why it is tightened in several steps and several passes.
watch: When investigating a leak, look at "was the preload introduced evenly" rather than "was the torque right". Even at the same torque, the preload differs from bolt to bolt.
Do not mix new and reused bolts, or different lots or different coatings, in one joint. K differs and the preload is uneven.
Check the torque wrench calibration interval and the calibration certificate (ISO 6789).
For important joints such as rotating machinery couplings and high-pressure flanges, consider elongation measurement or tensioning.
